lines.text: Painted caves and ancient ports, sultans and colonisers, independence, collapse and a slow rebuilding. This is the story of Somalia, on the Horn of Africa.
More than five thousand years ago, people painted the caves of Laas Geel, some of the oldest and best kept rock art in Africa.
By about the year 900, Mogadishu was growing as a trading port on the Indian Ocean. It is the capital today.
From around 1300 the Ajuran Sultanate ruled the coast and the river valleys for some four centuries.
Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, born in 1856, would lead the Dervish state and fight the British for twenty years.
From the 1880s, as European powers carved up Africa, Italy took the long southern coast of the Somali lands as its colony.
Meanwhile Britain made the north, facing the Gulf of Aden, a protectorate of its own, British Somaliland.
Siad Barre, a soldier born in 1919, would seize power in 1969 and rule for more than twenty years.
Nuruddin Farah, born in 1945, would become Somalia's best known novelist, author of Maps and Links.
Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, born in 1955, would one day lead the country as president.
In 1960 the British north and the Italian south joined in independence as one country, Somalia.
In 1983 Mo Farah was born in Mogadishu. Running for Britain, he would win four Olympic golds.
In 1991 Siad Barre fell, the state collapsed, and civil war spread, followed by famine and, later, al-Shabaab.
In 1993, in the Battle of Mogadishu, American soldiers were killed, and the United Nations mission soon collapsed.
From the paintings of Laas Geel to a nation rebuilding, Somalia's story is not over.
